cards.q: What are the four levels of analytics?
cards.a: Descriptive (what happened), diagnostic (why it happened), predictive (what will happen) and prescriptive (what to do about it). Each level answers a different question for the decision owner.

cards.q: What does SPARC stand for when you frame an analytics question, and what is the R?
cards.a: Scope, Purpose, Audience, Rules and Deadline. The R is Rules, meaning the metric definitions. Settle all five before opening the data, and send the brief back in writing.

cards.q: What does Excel return for =-2^2, and why?
cards.a: 4, not -4. Excel applies the unary minus before the exponent, so it reads (-2)^2. Python reads -2**2 as -(2**2) = -4. Write =-(2^2) when you mean -4.

cards.q: What goes wrong if you leave out the last argument of VLOOKUP?
cards.a: It defaults to approximate match, which silently returns wrong values on unsorted keys. Use FALSE for exact match, or XLOOKUP, which is exact by default. Use approximate match only for sorted bands.

cards.q: Why should a 16-digit account number be stored as text in Excel?
cards.a: Excel keeps only 15 significant digits for numbers, so IDs that differ in the 16th digit become identical, and long numbers show in scientific notation. Import such columns as Text.

cards.q: Which Excel tool: hit a target by changing one input, test many inputs, store named cases, optimise with limits?
cards.a: Goal Seek (one input, one target), Data Table (many input values side by side), Scenario Manager (named cases), Solver (optimise with constraints).

cards.q: A PivotTable shows old numbers after you edit the source data. Why, and what is good practice?
cards.a: A PivotTable is an interactive GROUP BY snapshot, so it must be refreshed. Build it from a Table (Ctrl+T) so new rows are included, and refresh after every data change.

cards.q: How do loc and iloc differ for slices?
cards.a: loc is label-based and includes the end label; iloc is position-based and excludes the end. With the default index, df.loc[0:2] returns 3 rows and df.iloc[0:2] returns 2.

cards.q: Why does an integer column become float when one value is missing, and how do you keep integers?
cards.a: NumPy integers cannot hold NaN, so pandas upcasts to float64. Use the nullable Int64 dtype (capital I) to keep whole numbers together with missing values.

cards.q: What is the difference between groupby().agg() and groupby().transform()?
cards.a: agg returns one row per group. transform returns a result as long as the input, aligned to the original rows, so you can add group medians or shares as new columns.

cards.q: What does the sum of an all-missing group return in pandas, and how do you change it?
cards.a: 0, not NaN, which can hide missing data. Use sum(min_count=1) to get NaN when a group has no valid values.

cards.q: In NumPy, what does axis=0 do in a sum?
cards.a: It collapses rows: it works down each column. axis=1 collapses columns, across each row. For a 3 x 4 array, sum(axis=0) has shape (4,) and sum(axis=1) has shape (3,).

cards.q: What happens when you add 1 to a NumPy int8 array holding 127, and how do you avoid it?
cards.a: It wraps silently to -128, with no error. Choose a dtype that fits the data range. Floats are inexact too (0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3), so compare them with np.isclose.

cards.q: What do MCAR, MAR and MNAR mean for missing data?
cards.a: Missing completely at random (unrelated to any data), at random (depends on other observed columns), not at random (depends on the missing value itself, such as high earners hiding income). Check missing rates by other columns.

cards.q: The mean is above the median. What does that suggest, and what do you report?
cards.a: A right-skewed distribution with a long upper tail. Report the median and percentiles, and consider a log scale, because a few large values pull the mean up.

cards.q: Which charts must start their axis at zero, and why?
cards.a: Bar charts, because length carries the value and a cut axis exaggerates differences. Lines may use a tighter range if it is labelled, since position and slope carry the message.

cards.q: How do you work out the pixel size of a saved matplotlib figure?
cards.a: Pixels = inches x dpi. A figsize of (8, 4.5) saved at dpi=200 is 1,600 x 900 pixels.

cards.q: How do you link both OrderDate and ShipDate to one date table in Power BI?
cards.a: Only one relationship can be active. Keep the other inactive (role-playing dates) and switch it on inside a measure with USERELATIONSHIP.

cards.q: What must be true of the key on the one side of a relationship, and which filter direction is usual?
cards.a: The key must be unique (a dimension key). Use one-to-many relationships with single-direction filtering from dimension to fact, and decide the grain of the fact table first.

cards.q: What is the difference between filter context and row context in DAX?
cards.a: A measure runs once per visual cell with that cell's filter context. A calculated column has row context only. CALCULATE changes the filters first, then evaluates; context transition turns the current row into filters.

cards.q: A slicer selects Colour = Blue. What does CALCULATE([Sales], Product[Colour] = "Red") return?
cards.a: Red sales. A column filter inside CALCULATE replaces any existing filter on that same column, so the slicer's Blue selection is overridden.

cards.q: What do ALL, ALLSELECTED and ALLEXCEPT each keep?
cards.a: ALL removes every filter (share of the whole company). ALLSELECTED keeps slicer selections (share of the visible total). ALLEXCEPT removes filters from every column except the ones you list.

cards.q: Can ALL() in a DAX measure remove row-level security, and who bypasses RLS?
cards.a: No: RLS filters are applied before the measure runs. Viewers obey RLS; users with edit rights in the workspace bypass it. Percent-of-total therefore needs an unsecured total table.

cards.q: How does a Tableau FIXED LOD expression treat dimension filters?
cards.a: It computes at the dimensions you name and ignores ordinary dimension filters. DAX CALCULATE also computes at a chosen grain. A Looker Studio blend behaves like a join and duplicates rows when the grain is wrong.

cards.q: Give the formulas for ARPU, lifetime, LTV, CAC and payback.
cards.a: ARPU = revenue / customers; lifetime = 1 / churn; LTV = ARPU x margin x lifetime; CAC = spend / new customers; payback = CAC / (ARPU x margin). ARPU 150, margin 40%, churn 5% gives LTV 1,200.

cards.q: Why count distinct users, not events, in a funnel, and how do you keep the step order in pandas?
cards.a: A user who views two products would count twice. Use groupby('step').user.nunique() then .reindex(order), because groupby sorts step names alphabetically. No step may exceed the one before it.

cards.q: Does a p-value tell you the chance that B is better than A?
cards.a: No. It is how surprising the data would be if there were no true difference. 'Not significant' with a small sample is not 'no effect': read the CI against the minimum detectable effect.

cards.q: How does the required sample size change if you halve the minimum detectable effect?
cards.a: It grows about four times, because n scales with 1/MDE squared. Also decide the metric and guardrails before launch, run whole weeks, look once, and check SRM first.

cards.q: What goes into an analysis memo, in order?
cards.a: Bottom line, key numbers, why, recommendation, risks, then an appendix. Always recommend something, and match your words to the strength of the evidence: 'increased', 'suggests', 'unclear'.

cards.q: A stakeholder keeps adding requests mid-project. How do you handle the scope creep?
cards.a: State the time cost of each addition and offer a choice: swap it for existing work, move the deadline, or do it later. Confirm the agreed brief in writing.

quiz.q: Orders rise 10% while average order value falls 10%. Using revenue = orders x AOV, what happens to revenue?
quiz.why: 1.10 x 0.90 = 0.99, so revenue is down 1%. The tempting 'unchanged' adds +10 and -10 percentage points, but percentage changes multiply. Splitting a metric into parts shows where a change comes from.
Excel applies the unary minus before the exponent, so it computes (-3)^2 = 9. The tempting -9 is the maths-class and Python answer. Use =-(3^2) when you mean -9.

quiz.q: A company's fiscal year starts in April and is named after the year it ends. What does =YEAR(EDATE(B2, 9)) return for B2 = 15 March 2025?
quiz.why: 15 March 2025 plus 9 months is 15 December 2025, so the fiscal year is 2025 (April 2024 to March 2025). A date of 15 April 2025 would give 2026. Adding 9 months pushes April and later into the next year.

quiz.q: Data starts in row 2. Which conditional-format rule colours the whole row when column G says Returned?
quiz.why: The $ locks the column so every cell in the row looks at column G, while the row number stays relative. Without it, each column checks its own cell. Locking both ($G$2) makes every row follow row 2.

quiz.q: In pandas 3, what does d[d.x > 0]['y'] = 1 do to the DataFrame d?
opts: It sets y to 1 for the matching rows
Nothing: chained assignment never works, so use d.loc[d.x > 0, 'y'] = 1
It sets y to 1 for every row
quiz.why: The first bracket returns a copy, and the assignment changes only that copy, so d keeps its old values. One .loc call with rows and column writes into d itself.

quiz.q: A sample has 10 values. Can any of them have a z-score above 3 when you use the sample standard deviation?
opts: No: the largest possible z-score is (n - 1) / sqrt(n) = 2.85
Yes, if the value is extreme enough
Only if the data are normal
quiz.why: With 9 equal values and one different, z is exactly 2.85, the ceiling for n = 10. A z > 3 rule can never flag anything in a sample this small, so use the IQR rule or the median for small samples.
int8 holds -128 to 127, so adding 1 wraps around silently to -128. NumPy does not raise an error for array arithmetic. Pick a dtype that fits the data, and test with np.iinfo.

quiz.q: An export taken on the 12th shows the latest month's revenue down 40%. What do you check first?
opts: Whether the formulas have an off-by-one error
Whether the last month is incomplete (12 days of data), then compare like for like or drop the partial period
quiz.why: An incomplete period creates a fake trend. Check the date coverage before chasing causes. Compare the same 12 days of earlier months, or exclude the partial month.

quiz.q: A figure of 8 x 4.5 inches is saved with dpi=200. What is its pixel size?
quiz.why: Pixels = inches x dpi, so 8 x 200 = 1,600 and 4.5 x 200 = 900. The tempting 800 x 450 is dpi=100, the default for the screen. Use a higher dpi for slides and print.

quiz.q: DimDate has one active relationship to FactSales[OrderDate]. You also need sales by ShipDate. What is the right approach?
opts: Add a second, inactive relationship on ShipDate and use USERELATIONSHIP in the measure
quiz.why: Power BI allows only one active relationship between two tables, and two active paths would be ambiguous. An inactive role-playing relationship switched on inside a measure keeps one date table for both.

quiz.q: A slicer selects Colour = Blue. What does CALCULATE([Sales], Product[Colour] = "Red") show?
quiz.why: A column filter inside CALCULATE replaces the existing filter on that column, so the slicer's Blue is overridden. The tempting 'blank' assumes the filters are combined with AND, which happens only across different columns.

quiz.q: Which function gives each product's share of the visible total while keeping the slicer selections?
quiz.why: ALLSELECTED removes the visual's own row filters but keeps slicer selections, so the denominator is the visible total. ALL would remove the slicers too and give share of the whole company.

quiz.q: A report page is 1,280 px wide with 20 px margins on both sides, 20 px gaps and three cards in a row. Using (W - 2m - (n - 1)g) / n, how wide is each card?
quiz.why: (1280 - 40 - 40) / 3 = 400. Forgetting either the margins or the gaps gives 413, forgetting both gives 427, and counting three gaps instead of two gives 393.

quiz.q: ARPU is Rs 150 per month, gross margin 40% and monthly churn 5%. What is the LTV?
quiz.why: Lifetime = 1 / 0.05 = 20 months, and LTV = 150 x 0.40 x 20 = 1,200. The tempting 3,000 is revenue over the lifetime (150 x 20), which ignores that only the 40% margin is profit.

quiz.q: Monthly churn is 3%. About what share of customers is lost in a year?
quiz.why: Customers left after 12 months = 0.97^12 = 0.694, so about 31% are lost. The tempting 36% is 12 x 3%, which ignores that churn applies to a shrinking base.

quiz.q: You halve the minimum detectable effect in an A/B test. About how does the required sample size change?
opts: It becomes about four times larger
quiz.why: Sample size scales with 1/MDE squared, so halving the MDE multiplies n by 4. Doubling is the tempting linear guess. Small effects need far more users.

quiz.q: A test with 200 users per arm gives p = 0.30, and a colleague says 'no effect'. What is wrong with that conclusion?
opts: Not significant with a small sample is not 'no effect': read the CI against the minimum detectable effect
Nothing: p above 0.05 proves no effect
p = 0.30 means a 30% chance that B is better
p = 0.30 proves that B is worse
quiz.why: A small sample may simply lack power, and the confidence interval may still include a business-relevant lift. A p-value is not the probability that B is better; it describes data under no difference.

quiz.q: In a meeting someone asks for a number you do not have. What is the best reply?
opts: "I do not know; I will confirm by Thursday 5 pm"
quiz.why: Admit the gap and commit to a time. A confident guess risks a wrong number sticking, and 'soon' has no deadline. Define the numbers you do present if challenged.
